design_detail: Report with three parts. (1) Cross-sectional comparison of cultured white blood cells from 18 patients with a history of taking LSD, all with a history of other drugs or medicines (Table 1), 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD (Table 3) and 14 drug-free controls, 2 of whom were left out after a viral illness that began within a day of sampling (Table 4); two replicate blood samples per person, coded, cultured in one laboratory and scored in another by one person; results as breaks per 100 cells. (2) Four children of three of the LSD patients, exposed to LSD before birth (Table 2), compared with the adult controls. (3) In vitro: white blood cells from 6 healthy people cultured for 72 hours with LSD-25 at 0.001 to 10 µg/ml for the last 4, 24 or 48 hours, against untreated cultures; coded slides; breaks per 100 cells, mitotic index and the distribution of breaks among chromosomes (Tables 5 and 6, Figure 2). One sampling time per person and none from before LSD; the only statistical test printed is a chi-square for the distribution of breaks in vitro.
can_establish: That in this laboratory, coded slides from 18 patients with a history of LSD and of other drugs or medicines showed more breaks (13.2 per 100 cells) than those of 12 controls without drugs (3.8); that 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD had rates similar to the LSD patients (12.6 on average); and that LSD added to cultured cells was followed by more breaks at every concentration and time tested, without a concentration-response.
cannot_establish: Whether LSD caused the excess in people: there was no sample from before LSD, recruitment and the source and content of the LSD are not described, every LSD patient had a history of other drugs or medicines and the paper's own group taking other drugs without LSD had similar rates, two controls with high rates were left out after the fact, and no statistical comparison is reported. The children were compared only with adults; the concentrations in the dish are not linked to levels in the body; and nothing was measured in germ cells, so nothing can be said about cancer, birth defects or inherited damage.

sample.recruitment: Not described for any group. The LSD group are called patients with a history of LSD ingestion (p. 1046); the third author was assistant director of the psychiatric division of Bellevue Hospital (p. 1043, footnote), and two of his papers are cited, one on untoward reactions to LSD that led to hospital admission (refs. 13 and 32, p. 1049), but where and how the patients, the 6 patients taking other drugs, the 14 controls and the 4 children were found, and how many declined, are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated for the people sampled. In vitro donors: healthy, with no history of prior drug ingestion, radiation exposure or recent viral infection (p. 1043). Two of the 14 controls were left out because a viral infection with high fever and diarrhoea began within 24 hours of their blood sampling; both had high break rates (p. 1046; Table 4).
sample.demographics: LSD group (Table 1, p. 1045): 12 men and 6 women aged 19 to 52 (mean 24.4, editors' calculation; all but one aged 19 to 29), all white (p. 1046). Controls kept (Table 4, p. 1046): 9 men and 3 women aged 22 to 55 (mean 29.2, editors' calculation), all white except one Black man; the two left out were women aged 37 and 23. Other-drug group (Table 3, p. 1045): 4 adults aged 20 to 34 (3 men, 1 woman) and 2 boys aged 9; 2 white and 4 Black. Children (Table 2, p. 1045): 2 girls and 2 boys aged 2 months to 5½ years.
sample.attrition: Two of the 14 controls left out (p. 1046). Cells scored per person ranged from 78 to 300 in the LSD group and from 100 to 314 among the controls (Tables 1 and 4), although the methods describe 4 to 6 cover slips of 50 metaphases each (p. 1044); the shortfall is not explained.
sample.selection_effects: Patients rather than a community sample, with recruitment undescribed; the LSD group was younger than the controls and all had used other drugs or medicines; the other-drug group mixes adults taking prescribed medicines (chlorpromazine in three up to the day of sampling), one man with a long history of several drugs and two 9-year-old boys; controls with high rates were removed after an illness that began after sampling, while infections in the other groups are not reported.

exposure.measurement: LSD use by history: the number of doses and the interval since the last dose for each patient (Table 1, p. 1045), the usual amount per occasion for the group (p. 1046) and other drugs according to the patients' histories (Table 1). Whether the LSD was given in treatment or obtained otherwise is not stated, and nothing was tested; no biological verification. Children: the number of maternal doses during pregnancy and other drugs used in pregnancy (Table 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As reported (Table 1, p. 1045): 2 to 300 doses; last dose 2 weeks to 8 months before sampling (1 month for 9 of the 18); usual amount 300 to 600 µg per occasion (p. 1046), with two patients marked as taking low doses (50 to 100 µg). Children (Table 2; p. 1046): 1 to 4 maternal doses; the two with high rates exposed in the third and fourth months of pregnancy, the two with low rates to low doses late in pregnancy. In vitro (p. 1043): 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1 and 10 µg/ml for the last 4, 24 or 48 hours of a 72-hour culture. In people the route is implied only by the word ingestion.
exposure.polysubstance: All 18 had a history of other drugs or medicines (Table 1; p. 1046): amphetamines 15, marijuana 14, other hallucinogens 12, phenothiazines 10 (chlorpromazine at the time of sampling in 2), opiates 5, barbiturates 4, cocaine 4 (editors' count); one patient (case 37) reported only phenothiazines and one (case 26) only marijuana. The authors report no apparent relation between the type or number of other drugs and the break rate (p. 1046), without a test. A separate group of 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD was sampled (Table 3).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 2 weeks to 8 months since the last LSD dose, by history (Table 1). Children: sampled 2 months to 5½ years after birth (Table 2).

comparison.controls: Twelve drug-free controls kept in the analysis (2.0 to 5.5 breaks per 100 cells; 102 breaks in 2674 cells, 3.8) after two with high rates (31.0 and 14.0) were left out for a viral illness beginning within 24 hours of sampling (Table 4, p. 1046); 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD (Table 3, p. 1045). The children were compared with the adult controls; no unexposed children were sampled. In vitro: untreated cultures from the same 6 donors (65 breaks in 1680 cells, 3.9; Table 5).
comparison.matching: The controls are said to have an age and sex distribution similar to that of the LSD patients (p. 1046); they were older on average (29.2 against 24.4 years) and included fewer women (3 of 12 against 6 of 18) (editors' calculation from Tables 1 and 4).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No sample from before LSD use; psychiatric diagnoses, infections, x-ray exposure, smoking and alcohol are not reported for the LSD group or the other-drug group.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The controls are described as drug-free, without drug ingestion (p. 1046); alcohol, tobacco and medicines are not detailed.

outcomes.instruments: In people: two drops of capillary blood in microculture tubes, 72 hours at 37°C, vinblastine for the last 2 hours; cultures and slides made in another laboratory (K. H.), the samples coded by W. A. F. and the coded slides sent to Buffalo (M. M. C.); 4 to 6 cover slips per person, mounted at random two to a slide; 50 well-spread metaphases per cover slip chosen at ×250 by workers not involved in scoring; one person analysed the cells at ×2500, as in the in vitro study (pp. 1043–1044). In vitro: whole-blood microcultures, colcemide for the last 2 hours, aceto-orcein stain and phase-contrast microscopy; duplicate cultures of each treatment, two slides each, aiming at 100 cells per treatment per donor; mitotic index from 250 cells per slide (p. 1043).
outcomes.validity_norms: Chromatid and isochromatid breaks counted as single breaks, exchange figures and dicentrics as two; gaps noted but not counted (p. 1043); the two classes of break were combined deliberately (p. 1047). Results are breaks per 100 cells ('per cent breaks', with breaks over cells scored in brackets, Tables 1 to 4), not a share of cells, although Table 5's footnote and the text on case 15 call the figures percentages of cells. The authors call their control rate almost identical to that of the in vitro controls and to earlier published findings (p. 1046).
outcomes.operationalization: Per person, the number of breaks in the cells scored; 'increased' means above the control mean (p. 1046). In vitro, breaks per 100 cells for each concentration and time, the mitotic index and the distribution of breaks across chromosome groups (Tables 5 and 6, Figure 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The only test printed is a chi-square for the distribution of breaks among chromosome groups in vitro (Table 6); the significant mitotic inhibition and the highly significant excess in the LSD patients are reported without a named test.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Coded slides, cells chosen by workers not involved in scoring, and one scorer (p. 1044); in vitro slides coded and evaluated blind (p. 1043). When the code was broken, and whether the two controls were left out before or after decoding, is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: As printed: LSD patients 13.2 breaks per 100 cells (566 in 4282) against 3.8 (102 in 2674) in 12 controls, called more than three times the control mean and highly significant, without a test (p. 1046). Editors' calculations from Tables 1 and 4: per-person means 13.2 (SD 6.0) against 3.9 (SD 1.2), a difference of 9.3 (Welch 95% interval 6.2 to 12.3; Mann-Whitney P < 0.001); 16 of 18 above the highest control (5.5) and 2 within the control range (5.3 and 5.5). With the two controls left out after a viral illness included: 5.4 (161 in 2974), a difference of 6.6 (1.5 to 11.7). Other-drug group (Table 3): mean of the six rates 12.6 (161 breaks in 1361 cells, 11.8), no different from the LSD group (Mann-Whitney P = 0.84; difference -0.6, 95% interval -7.3 to 6.1) and above the controls (P = 0.008); the paper itself makes neither comparison. Within the LSD group: no rank correlation of the break rate with the number of doses (-0.01) or with months since the last dose (0.10); the 10 with phenothiazines in their history 12.6 per 100 cells, the 8 without 14.0 (pooled counts). Children: 119 breaks in 1000 cells (11.9). In vitro (Table 5): 1009 breaks in 7735 treated cells (13.0) against 65 in 1680 (3.9), 7.7 to 17.5 across the 15 conditions with no consistent concentration-response; mitotic index 6.2% in controls and about 3.0% to 4.7% in treated cultures (Figure 2, editors' reading); breaks among chromosome groups chi-square 209.01, df 8, P < 0.001 (Table 6).
analysis.selective_reporting: No test statistic for the main comparison in people or for the in vitro break rates; per-person cell counts below the number the methods describe are not explained; infections were looked for in the controls but are not reported for the other groups; the six patients taking other drugs are described but compared neither with the LSD group nor with the controls.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Patients with a history of LSD and of other drugs or medicines had about three times the break rate of 12 drug-free controls, and so did patients taking chlorpromazine or other drugs without LSD; LSD added to cultured cells was followed by more breaks at every concentration, without a concentration-response; two of four children exposed before birth had high rates, compared only with adults.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The discussion states that "It is now apparent that LSD is capable of causing chromosomal damage" in cells in a dish and in the circulating white blood cells of people who take it (p. 1047, Discussion, 2nd paragraph). It takes the match between the patients' rates and those at 0.001 and 0.01 µg/ml as showing the concentrations cells meet in the body, although every concentration gave similar rates (p. 1047); it reads the children's results as evidence that LSD crosses the placenta and raises the possibility of birth defects, leukaemia and damage to germ cells passed on for generations (p. 1048, Discussion, 7th, 8th and 10th paragraphs), none of which was measured. It notes that 8 of the 18 had taken no phenothiazines yet had raised rates, and that the patients taking chlorpromazine without LSD also had raised rates (pp. 1047–1048), but it does not compare its other-drug group with the LSD group, whose rates were similar.

timeline.event: Cohen, Marinello and Back, the same laboratory: LSD added to cultured white blood cells of two donors at the same five concentrations and three exposure times raised breaks per cell; one man with schizophrenia had 12 percent breakage in 200 cells 8 months after 15 LSD treatments (ref. 2 of this paper).

Irwin and Egozcue: about twice the break rate in 8 volunteers who reported taking LSD as in 9 who had not (23.6 against 11.9 breaks per 100 cells, editors' calculation from their Table 2); cited here for its dicentric chromosomes (ref. 3).
Loughman et al.: no chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people reporting heavy illicit LSD use, scored by someone who did not know their drug histories.

Sparkes et al.: no significant difference in breaks between 8 people exposed to LSD and 4 controls; they note that the laboratories reporting damage had higher control rates and less complete culture media.

The same group's later report (Cohen, Hirschhorn, Verbo and colleagues): 13 of 14 adults exposed to illicit LSD above the control mean (7.53% against 1.20%), and 9.2% in nine children exposed before birth against 4.0% in four whose mothers took LSD only before pregnancy; three adults of the present report not counted again (as described by Dishotsky et al., 1971, p. 433 and Table 2; not read).
Tjio et al.: 32 hospital patients sampled before and after one dose of pharmaceutical LSD, slides scored blind: no significant change in the share of cells with aberrations.

Dishotsky et al., review: lists this report as positive in vitro (Table 1, p. 432: 8725 treated cells, 7.7 to 17.5%; this report's Table 5 sums to 7735, editors' sum) and says it found a significant increase at the lowest concentration and shortest exposure, which Tjio did not confirm (p. 431), although no test is given here; lists it as positive in people (Table 2, p. 433: 18 people exposed to illicit LSD, 4282 cells, 13.2% against 3.8% in 12 controls), although this report does not say where its patients' LSD came from; and uses its 6 patients taking other drugs (12.6%, not significantly different from 13.2%, p. 434) to attribute raised breakage to drug use in general.

replication.where_it_stands: The excess in people was reported by two laboratories in 1967 and 1968 (this one and Irwin and Egozcue's) and not by others with lower control rates or before-and-after samples (Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969). This report's own group taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had similar rates, the basis of the 1971 review's conclusion that the raised rates reflected drug use in general rather than LSD. Its in vitro increase, without a concentration-response, may include the cultures of the same laboratory's earlier report, which the review counts as a separate study. No study read here sampled people before and after LSD with an unexposed group sampled at the same times.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Maimon M. Cohen: Division of Human Genetics, Department of Pediatrics, State University of New York at Buffalo School of Medicine, and Buffalo Children's Hospital; Kurt Hirschhorn: Division of Medical Genetics, Mount Sinai School of Medicine, New York City Health Research Council Career Scientist; William A. The first author also led the earlier report on cells in a dish and one patient (Cohen, Marinello and Back, 1967, ref. 2).

what_would_settle_it: Blood samples from the same people before and after LSD of known content, with comparison groups matched for age, sex and other drugs and medicines (chlorpromazine in particular) and sampled at the same times, infections recorded in every group in advance, rules for excluding samples fixed before decoding, slides scored blind by more than one reader and a pre-specified statistical comparison; for children, unexposed children of the same ages; for inherited risk, studies of germ cells rather than blood cells.

domains.note: No adjustment. Every LSD patient had a history of other drugs or medicines (amphetamines 15 of 18, phenothiazines 10), and the paper's own group taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had similar rates, so confounding could account for the whole excess; the controls were older and included fewer women; infections, x-rays and psychiatric illness are not reported for the patients.
LSD use by history; source, content and amounts unknown; no verification.
Recruitment of patients, controls and children not described; patients rather than a community sample.

Phenothiazines, which the authors say are often given to end a difficult LSD experience, in 10 of 18 (2 at sampling); patients taking chlorpromazine without LSD had raised rates, although the 8 without phenothiazines also had raised rates.

Two of 14 controls left out after an illness that began after sampling (including them reduces the difference from 9.3 to 6.6 breaks per 100 cells, editors' calculation); fewer cells than the methods describe for several people.

Coded slides, cells chosen by others and one scorer are strengths; but the measure is labelled inconsistently, chromatid lesions that can arise in culture dominate, and when the code was broken relative to the exclusions is not stated.
No test for the main comparisons; the comparison of the LSD group with the other-drug group, which the data allow, is not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E for an observational comparison of exposed and unexposed people. Coded slides scored by one person, cells chosen by others, and complete, internally consistent tables (every rate matches its counts, and Tables 5 and 6 agree on 1009 breaks) are strengths, so the rates are credible as measurements. The overall judgment is very high because the comparison of LSD patients with drug-free controls cannot separate LSD from the other drugs and medicines every patient had taken: the paper's own patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had similar rates. Recruitment, the source of the LSD and infections in the patients are not described, two controls with high rates were left out after the fact, and no statistical comparison is reported. A second reader may judge confounding high rather than very high; the overall judgment is at least high either way. Citable for: the break rates with denominators in each group, including the similar rates in the other-drug group; the in vitro rates and the absence of a concentration-response; the children's rates as observations. Not citable for: LSD causing chromosome damage in people, the concentrations reached in the body, or any risk of cancer, birth defects or inherited damage.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Human peripheral blood white cells in 72-hour whole-blood microcultures from 6 healthy people (3 men, 3 women) with no history of prior drug ingestion, radiation exposure or recent viral infection (p. 1043). Whether they include the two donors of the same laboratory's earlier report is not stated.
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: LSD-25 in sterile distilled water added at final concentrations of 10, 1, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 µg/ml 48, 24 or 4 hours before harvest of 72-hour cultures; colcemide for the last 2 hours; duplicate cultures of each treatment; untreated cultures as controls (p. 1043).
preclinical.human_equivalent_dose_basis: None measured. The authors infer from the similar break rates that 0.001 to 0.01 µg/ml corresponds to what cells meet in the body (p. 1047), an inference Table 5 cannot support, because all five concentrations gave similar rates.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: No: dividing cells kept at a fixed concentration for hours in a dish; the authors themselves note the difficulty of extrapolating from cells in a dish to people (p. 1047).

key_findings.finding: Sampling and blinding: cultures from 22 people who had taken LSD (Table 1) or been exposed to it before birth (Table 2), 6 patients taking other drugs but no LSD (Table 3) and 14 drug-free controls (Table 4); two replicate blood samples per person, collected and coded by one author (W. A. F.); cultures and slides made in another laboratory (K. H.); the coded slides sent to Buffalo (M. M. C.), where workers not involved in scoring chose 50 well-spread metaphases per cover slip on 4 to 6 cover slips per person, and one person analysed them. Specimens from several people were cultured twice.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › In Vivo Studies, 1st paragraph (p. 1043, right column, continuing on p. 1044, left column)

key_findings.finding: Table 1, 18 patients with a history of LSD (12 men, 6 women, aged 19 to 52; 2 to 300 doses; last dose 2 weeks to 8 months before sampling): breaks per 100 cells from 5.3 (16 in 300) to 25.1 (44 in 175); in all, 566 breaks in 4282 cells (13.2). All were white and all had a history of other drugs; 2 (cases 6 and 28) were taking chlorpromazine when sampled. The usual amount per occasion was 300 to 600 µg.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 1045); Results › In Vivo Studies, 2nd paragraph (p. 1046, left column, continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Controls, Table 4: of 14 people without drug ingestion, said to be of similar age and sex distribution, two women (cases 4 and 13) developed a viral infection with high fever and diarrhoea within 24 hours of sampling and had 31.0 (31 in 100) and 14.0 (28 in 200) breaks per 100 cells; they were left out. The other 12 had 2.0 to 5.5 (102 breaks in 2674 cells, 3.8), which the authors call almost identical to their in vitro controls and earlier published findings.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 and footnotes; Results › In Vivo Studies, 1st paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: controls kept 9 men and 3 women, mean age 29.2, against 12 men and 6 women, mean age 24.4, in the LSD group. With the two controls left out included, the controls' rate is 5.4 (161 in 2974).

key_findings.finding: The authors report that every LSD patient was above the control mean, that the increase was more than three times the control mean and highly significant (no test or statistic given), that there was no apparent correlation of the break rate with the number of doses, the amount per dose or the interval since the last dose, and no apparent relation with the type or number of other drugs; 12 dicentrics and 5 exchange figures were seen in the LSD group and no structural rearrangements in the controls.
key_findings.locator: Results › In Vivo Studies, 2nd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculations from Tables 1 and 4: per-person means 13.2 (SD 6.0) against 3.9 (SD 1.2), difference 9.3 (Welch 95% interval 6.2 to 12.3; Mann-Whitney P < 0.001); 16 of 18 above the highest control (5.5), 2 within the control range (cases 28 and 29, 5.3 and 5.5). With the two controls left out included: difference 6.6 (1.5 to 11.7). Spearman rank correlation of the break rate with the number of doses -0.01 and with months since the last dose 0.10.

key_findings.finding: Other drugs in the LSD group by history (Table 1 key): amphetamines in 15 of 18, marijuana 14, other hallucinogens 12, phenothiazines 10 (2 at the time of sampling), opiates 5, barbiturates 4, cocaine 4; case 37 reported only phenothiazines and case 26 only marijuana.
key_findings.note: Editors' count. Pooled break rates: 10 with phenothiazines in their history 12.6 per 100 cells (editors' calculation), 8 without 14.0.

key_findings.finding: Table 3, six patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD: three taking chlorpromazine up to the day of sampling, 17.4 (34 in 195), 21.5 (43 in 200) and 13.7 (28 in 205) breaks per 100 cells; a man with a history of amphetamines, opiates, marijuana and barbiturates, 9.0 (18 in 200); a 9-year-old boy taking diphenhydramine, 10.0 (26 in 261); and a 9-year-old boy given chlorpromazine and thioridazine until a month before sampling and diphenhydramine in the last week, born with opioid dependence after exposure throughout pregnancy, 4.0 (12 in 300). The authors say the patients receiving chlorpromazine showed a marked increase, that 8 of the 18 LSD patients had no phenothiazines and still showed raised rates, that a combined effect of the two drugs cannot be judged, and that controlled studies of chlorpromazine are in progress.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (p. 1045); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 1047, right column, continuing on p. 1048, left column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: mean of the six rates 12.6 (161 breaks in 1361 cells, 11.8), no different from the 18 LSD patients (Mann-Whitney P = 0.84; difference -0.6, 95% interval -7.3 to 6.1) and higher than the 12 controls (P = 0.008). The paper reports neither comparison; the 1971 review's 'not significantly different' (Dishotsky et al., 1971, p. 434) is the review's own.

key_findings.finding: Children exposed before birth (Table 2), four children of three mothers listed by number (2, 14 and 9), numbers that match three of the women in Table 1 (mother 9 is marked as taking low doses in both tables): a girl of 11 months, 4 maternal doses, also amphetamines, cocaine and marijuana in pregnancy, 19.0 (57 in 300); a boy of 2½ years, 1 dose, no other drugs, 13.0 (39 in 300); a girl of 5½ years, 2 doses, marijuana, 7.5 (15 in 200); a boy of 2 months, 4 doses, cocaine and marijuana, 4.0 (8 in 200); in all 119 breaks in 1000 cells (11.9). The two with high rates were exposed in the third and fourth months of pregnancy to the usual amounts, the two with low rates (the same mother) to low doses late in pregnancy. No obvious physical or behavioural abnormalities had been noted in the four children.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 1045); Results › In Vivo Studies, 3rd paragraph (p. 1046, right column); Discussion, 9th paragraph (p. 1048, right column)
key_findings.note: No unexposed children were sampled; the children are compared with adult controls.

key_findings.finding: In vitro, Table 5 (cells pooled from 6 donors, which the authors say did not differ significantly from each other or by sex, without data): breaks per 100 cells after 48 hours 12.6, 7.7, 17.5, 10.7 and 12.5 at 10, 1, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 µg/ml; after 24 hours 11.5, 15.8, 13.0, 15.4 and 10.8; after 4 hours 17.1, 10.6, 13.1, 15.2 and 11.2 (65 breaks in 578 cells at 0.001 µg/ml); untreated cultures 3.9 (65 in 1680). The text calls the lowest treated rate almost twice the control and the highest over four times; no test is reported. Most aberrations were chromatid and isochromatid breaks, with a few chromatid exchanges and dicentrics and no rings.
key_findings.locator: Results › In Vitro Studies, 2nd paragraph (p. 1044, left column, continuing in the right column); Table 5 (p. 1046)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 1009 breaks in 7735 treated cells (13.0); the highest rate falls at a different concentration for each exposure time, so there is no concentration-response over a 10,000-fold range. Every condition has more cells and more breaks than the same condition in the laboratory's earlier report (Cohen, Marinello and Back, 1967, Table 1, p. 1417), and the highest rate at each exposure time falls at the same concentration in both (0.1 µg/ml at 48 hours, 1 µg/ml at 24 hours, 10 µg/ml at 4 hours), consistent with the earlier cultures being pooled here, which the paper does not say.

key_findings.finding: Mitotic index: 16,000 cells scored on control slides and about 6000 per treatment; mitosis 6.2% in controls; the authors report significant inhibition at every concentration (no test given), greater with longer exposure (Figure 2: treated cultures about 3.0% to 4.7%, editors' reading). They note that the inhibition was not as obvious in people.
key_findings.locator: Results › In Vitro Studies, 1st paragraph (p. 1044, left column); Figure 2 (p. 1044); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 1047, left column)

key_findings.finding: Distribution of breaks in vitro (Table 6): 930 breaks assigned to chromosomes and 79 unidentifiable; more than expected from chromosome length on chromosome 1 (154 against 80.82), chromosome 2 (119 against 75.70) and group C (420 against 346.52), fewer in groups D, E, F and G; chi-square 209.01, df 8, P < 0.001. Breaks clustered near centromeres and in regions the authors describe as secondary constrictions.
key_findings.locator: Results › In Vitro Studies, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 1045, left column, continuing in the right column and on p. 1046); Table 6 (p. 1047); Figure 3 (p. 1046)
key_findings.note: Editors' check: 930 + 79 = 1009, the sum of the treated breaks in Table 5, so Table 6 covers the in vitro cultures only. The test treats each break as independent, although breaks cluster within cells, cultures and donors.

key_findings.finding: Agreement between replicates, as reported: one control (case 30) 1, 2, 2, 1 and 1 breaks per 50 metaphases on five cover slips from two tubes; another control (case 19) 5 in 100 and 6 in 100 in successive cultures; an LSD patient (case 36) 9/50, 11/45, 9/36, 12/50, 8/50 and 9/33 on six cover slips; a child exposed before birth (case 1) 24 in 100 and 33 in 200 in successive cultures. The authors call the agreement close.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the child's two cultures gave 24% and 16.5% (chi-square P = 0.16), a difference close to the 9.3-point difference between the LSD group and the controls.

key_findings.finding: The authors' conclusions: "It is now apparent that LSD is capable of causing chromosomal damage" in cells in a dish and in people's circulating white blood cells; yields in people and in the dish were comparable, and the match of the patients' mean with 0.001 and 0.01 µg/ml supports, in their view, that these are the concentrations cells meet in the body. They go on to a possible future increase in leukaemia, congenital defects through transplacental transport, and damage to germ cells whose consequences may appear only after several generations; none of these was studied.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 1047, left column); 7th, 8th and 10th paragraphs (p. 1048); Summary (p. 1048, right column, continuing on p. 1049)

key_findings.finding: Case 37 in Table 1 is a man of 52 with 15 doses of LSD, the last 8 months before sampling, phenothiazines as his only other drug, and 13.0 breaks per 100 cells (39 in 300). The paper does not say whether he is the patient of its ref. 2; it presents itself as extending that report with a significant sample of patients.
key_findings.locator: Opening paragraph (p. 1043, left column); Table 1, case 37 (p. 1045)
key_findings.note: Editors' comparison with Cohen, Marinello and Back (1967, p. 1418): a man of 51 with paranoid schizophrenia, 15 LSD treatments with psychotherapy from 1960 to 1966, sampled 8 months after the last, also treated with chlorpromazine and chlordiazepoxide, 12 percent breakage in 200 cells. Sex, number of treatments, interval and phenothiazine treatment match; age and the number of cells differ.

reporting_issues.issue: The measure is labelled inconsistently: Tables 1 to 4 give 'per cent breaks' as breaks over cells scored (Table 4 footnote), but Table 5's footnote calls its percentages '% of cells with breaks', the text calls the in vitro control rate a percentage of cells with abnormalities, and the discussion calls case 15's 13.0 the percentage of cells with damage. Table 5's numerators sum to 1009, the number of breaks distributed in Table 6, so they are breaks.
reporting_issues.consequence: All figures are breaks per 100 cells; comparisons with studies that count the share of cells with an aberration (Tjio et al., 1969) are not like with like.

reporting_issues.issue: No statistical test is given for the main comparison in people ('highly significant'), for the in vitro break rates, for the mitotic inhibition ('significant') or for the absence of differences between the six donors; the only test printed, the chi-square of Table 6, treats 930 breaks as independent.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size and precision of the differences had to be recomputed (editors' calculations); Table 6's P < 0.001 overstates the certainty.

reporting_issues.issue: Two controls with high rates (31.0 and 14.0) were left out because a viral illness began within 24 hours of their sampling; the paper does not say when this decision was made or whether infections were looked for in the LSD and other-drug groups (the 1971 review calls the two retrospectively eliminated, p. 433).
reporting_issues.consequence: Including them lowers the difference from 9.3 to 6.6 breaks per 100 cells (editors' calculation) but does not remove it; the exclusion rule was applied to one group only.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods describe 4 to 6 cover slips of 50 metaphases per person (p. 1044), but five LSD patients had fewer than 200 cells scored (78 to 184) and so did two controls (100 and 182) and one excluded control (100) (Tables 1 and 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; some rates rest on few cells (case 2: 5 breaks in 78 cells).

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion takes the match between the patients' mean rate and the rates at 0.001 and 0.01 µg/ml as support that these are the concentrations cells meet in the body (p. 1047), but in Table 5 all five concentrations from 0.001 to 10 µg/ml gave similar rates (10.6 to 17.5, apart from 7.7).
reporting_issues.consequence: With no concentration-response, matching rates cannot identify the concentration reached in the body.

reporting_issues.issue: The group taking other drugs but no LSD is presented as exposed to the kinds of drugs LSD patients take (p. 1047), but four of the six were taking prescribed medicines (chlorpromazine, thioridazine, diphenhydramine), two were boys of 9 and only one had a history of several non-medical drugs (Table 3); the group is not compared with the LSD group, whose rates were similar.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's own data do not separate LSD from other drugs and medicines; the comparison is left to the reader and was later made, without a stated test, by the 1971 review.

reporting_issues.issue: Replicates are said to agree closely (p. 1047), but the child's two successive cultures gave 24 and 16.5 breaks per 100 cells.
reporting_issues.consequence: Within-person variation between cultures can be of the same size as the group difference; one culture per person can misplace a person by several points.

reporting_issues.issue: The children (aged 2 months to 5½ years) are compared only with adult controls (Table 4), and their raised rates are read as evidence that LSD crosses the placenta (p. 1048).
reporting_issues.consequence: Without unexposed children of the same ages, and with other drugs in pregnancy for three of the four, the children's rates cannot be attributed to LSD.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper does not say whether case 37 of Table 1 is the single patient of its own earlier report (ref. 2), whom he matches in sex, number of LSD treatments, interval since the last and phenothiazine treatment, nor whether the in vitro data of Table 5 include the earlier report's cultures, which every condition's larger counts and identical peak concentrations would allow.
reporting_issues.consequence: If either overlap holds, the two reports are not independent; the 1971 review counts both reports' in vitro data as separate studies (Table 1, p. 432) and would count the patient twice, once among 126 people given pharmaceutical LSD (Table 3, p. 433) and once among 184 exposed to illicit LSD (Table 2, p. 433).

verification.source_read: PDF scan (version of record, NEJM archive copy), N Engl J Med 277(20):1043–1049, all seven pages (no cover page; the article fills pp. 1043–1049). The PDF has no text layer for the article, so every number was read on pages rendered at 150 dpi, and Tables 1 to 6, Figure 2 and the running text again at 300 dpi; an OCR text made in the scratch folder was used only to search. For the comparisons with the earlier report, pp. 1417–1418 of Cohen, Marinello and Back (1967, Science 155) were read on rendered pages (Table 1 at 300 dpi). No supplement.
